summary: The Open Metaverse Browser is the Metaverse Standards Forum's own attempt at a neutral client for spatial content, and it is the only subject on this map that is a working browser with a downloadable binary and a documented module interface. Read the parts separately, because they are not governed alike. Sneeze, the engine, is Apache-2.0 and lives under the Forum's GitHub organisation; RCSF, a canonical skeleton mapping across fifteen formats, is Forum-hosted and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Everything else is Metaversal Corporation's: Rubidium, the browser you actually run, is proprietary with all rights reserved; the Halogen renderer, the RMAP networking library, the Map library and the WebAssembly SDKs are the vendor's repositories, and Sneeze pins all of them. SneezeSDK is the module-writing half of that split, and it is the only published contract this subject has: an Apache-2.0 C header that fixes the whole guest-to-engine wire format, a language-neutral reference with one page per class, and per-language bindings carried as submodules. It is not Forum-governed — it sits under MetaversalCorp — yet it is what a second implementer would have to build against, because the engine ships no specification of the fabric format. This file scores the SDK at its `prep` branch, head `4239e2b`, 18 August 2026. That branch differs from `main` in documentation only: it adds first-run guides for Linux, macOS and Windows, and it is behind `main` on the version file, on the versioning rule the front page used to state, and on four of the five binding pins. Count the bindings carefully — the front page marks five available, while the SDK's own reference and its porting guide both still say three. Three things a standards audience should not take on trust. Signature verification is called and its result thrown away, so an unverified fabric loads and runs; the trust level a module reads is then overwritten with a constant before it is stored, so it reports the same value whatever the certificate said. There is no resource budget at all, no fuel, no deadline and no memory ceiling, although the project's own wiki promises each fabric a CPU budget. And there is no format specification and no conformance suite, so the only definition of the format is the engine — and inside the SDK the C reference already contradicts the header it says it layers on, describing the fabric's services as an indexed list in the open snapshot where every other page says they are keyed by name and deliberately kept out of it. Whole planes are simply absent: no audio, no physics, no avatar, no geospatial anything, no credential of any kind, and immersive sessions are a runtime probe rather than a session. Buildable today from public sources: Sneeze, its SDKs and Halogen, pinned to public dependencies — except that Sneeze links the vendor's Map library, whose own README says it configures but does not yet compile, and which ships with no licence file at all.

coverage.note: The engine does not own a pipeline. It builds draw lists on a compositor thread and hands them to an ANARI device, which decides how to draw them; the shipping device is Halogen, an ANARI implementation over Google Filament. Geometry reaches the device as spheres, curves, boxes, panels and triangle meshes, and the frame is either read back to a buffer or drawn straight into a Vulkan swapchain on a native window.

coverage.note: Sneeze targets no low-level graphics interface itself; it targets ANARI and lets the loaded device choose. Vulkan, Metal and DX12 appear only inside Halogen's Filament backend and inside the separate Vox compute path. A standards reader should note the consequence: swapping the renderer is a library-name change, but nothing in the browser states which interface a given build actually used.

coverage.note: Two channels: scene-global ambient and directional light authored in the fabric's optional Primary block, and placed point or spot lights authored as light nodes. Halogen adds soft shadows and a default image-based light. There is no global illumination, no probes and no baking. One composition rule is worth a working group's attention: a placed light's intensity is multiplied by the square of its world scale times the per-scene render scale, so illumination survives being embedded in another fabric.

coverage.note: The scene object model is the centre of the design and is offered as the spatial answer to the document object model. A scene owns a structural root fabric; each fabric owns a tree of nodes; each node points at a map object that carries the spatial payload. Node handles are per-container, not scene-global, so two unrelated publishers cannot collide.

coverage.note: Every node composes a full translation, rotation and scale in 64-bit floats and inherits its parent's frame, with no class-specific shortcut. The convention is published, and more plainly than the engine source suggests: the module documentation states a right-handed world frame with X east, Y north and Z up, on both the node and the builder pages, so an author writing a module has a contract to work from. The gap is the file. The fabric manifest still carries no axis or handedness declaration, so nothing about the frame travels with the content and a second implementation has to be told out of band. The SDK quotes are from the `prep` branch, identical there to `main`.

The scene itself lives under `Data.Scene` as a node tree nested through `aChildren`. The browser reads it and the browser also writes it, from the command line.

coverage.note: The format encodes no meshes. A node names an external resource by a 128-byte reference string, the browser fetches it and decides what it is by sniffing the bytes, and a glTF or binary glTF file is parsed with fastgltf into a renderer-agnostic model. Only the default scene is read. The MetaversalCorp copy adds Draco and meshoptimizer decode units; the Forum copy has neither.

coverage.note: Composition is the strongest part of the design. Any node may set its subtype to 255, at which point its resource reference is read as the address of another fabric; the browser fetches that fabric, opens a container for its identity and grafts its tree under the attachment node. Fabrics therefore nest to any depth from independent publishers, and the same construct loads the root fabric, so root and attachment point are one mechanism.

coverage.note: Geometry is accumulated in metres and a panel's world size is authored in metres, which is a real unit agreement. The part that is missing is any declaration: the manifest has no units field, and after traversal the whole scene is multiplied by one factor chosen so its extent fits a fixed render volume of five units. Body radii are then magnified by a power law and moons are pushed outward by a hard-coded factor, so what is drawn is deliberately not to scale. The module contract does not help either: the position, scale and bound setters an author calls take bare 64-bit floats, and the documentation that names their frame names no unit at all. The SDK quote is from the `prep` branch, identical there to `main`.

Navigating destroys the whole tree and rebuilds it from the new address with no camera continuity and no state carried across, and the engine's own note says two things about doing it: an in-flight fabric fetch is not cancelled so the completion callback runs against freed memory, and the teardown is not synchronised with the compositor so navigating while rendering can crash. coverage.note: The opposite of selective disclosure. Every module a fabric loads is handed the whole container identity record when it opens — the persona's name and its hash, the organisation's name and its hash, the signing certificate's fingerprint and the trust level — with no scoping, no consent step and no way to hand over less. The persona half is the person using the browser: the engine's own note calls it a first and last name typed locally, a local testing proxy. There is nothing to disclose selectively with, because there is no credential, and nothing to withhold with, because the record arrives whole. coverage.note: Nothing expresses a position against the Earth. A search of the engine for the usual vocabulary — a geodetic datum, a latitude, a coordinate reference code — returns nothing. Positions are Cartesian doubles in the fabric's own frame, with an orbital model for celestial bodies. The project names the Open Geospatial Consortium as an aligned body; no geospatial code has landed. The project's own architecture proposal, version 2026.Q2.0, names GeoPose 1.0 from the Open Geospatial Consortium as the intended encoding for real-world position and orientation, so this is a described plan rather than an unclaimed gap.

coverage.note: World logic is WebAssembly compiled by Wasmtime, and the interface is the most carefully designed thing in this subject. Every guest request crosses a single import called `Call` carrying a self-describing packet routed by a subsystem number and a method number, so adding a method is adding a number and a module compiled once keeps loading as the engine grows. The guest supplies seven exports. The `prep` branch is what makes this reproducible by an outsider: it adds first-run guides for Linux, macOS and Windows that take a reader from an empty folder to a module with the right shape, importing only `Sneeze.Call` and exporting the seven symbols. Count the bindings carefully, though — the front page marks five available, while the SDK's own reference and its porting guide both still say three.

coverage.note: The isolation that exists is genuine: one Wasmtime store per persona, signer and container so unrelated publishers cannot share memory; every payload read bounds-checked against the declared size with an exact-consumption rule that rejects an over- or under-sized packet without side effects; SPIR-V validated before it reaches a driver. Two holes are large. The engine's own ownership checks have no callers. And the load path calls signature and chain verification, discards both results, and opens the fabric and runs its modules either way — verification is recorded, never enforced.

coverage.note: The fabric format carries no version field. The ABI's version constant covers the packet framing only and is explicitly not bumped when methods are added. The consequences are already live and the vendor says so: the release notes tell authors that fabrics made before this release must be updated and that the format will not be stable until version 1.0.0. The drift is visible in the shipped corpus — the engine's own note says the services block is a name-keyed object and every accessor tests for one, while the published tutorial fabrics ship an empty array, which the engine reads as no services and reports no error. The module interface is the opposite story and deserves the credit: method numbers are permanent, monotonic and append-only, superseded methods stay in the header so already-deployed modules keep running, and the version constant is documented as covering the packet framing alone. This subject therefore has an exemplary update rule for its code interface and none at all for its content format. The SDK quotes are from the `prep` branch, identical there to `main`.

coverage.note: There is no specification of the fabric format, no interface document beyond the ABI header, and no conformance suite. The test executable covers engine subsystems — signing, storage, cache, shader validation, compute, the clock — which proves the implementation works, not that a second implementation would agree with it. The cost of having no suite is already visible inside the SDK itself. The reference for the C binding documents the fabric's services as an indexed list read out of the open snapshot, with a count and per-index name, type and endpoint getters; every other page, and the header, say services are keyed by name, served on demand, and deliberately kept out of the snapshot. So two bindings of one interface describe the same block two incompatible ways. Separately, the C reference and the new quickstart both teach the scene method numbers the header marks deprecated. Nothing tests for either. Until a format document and a suite exist, compatible with this browser has no testable meaning. The SDK quotes are from the `prep` branch, identical there to `main`.

coverage.note: The Open Metaverse Browser loads and displays spatial content from multiple formats, with native scene composition. It can host content from different sources within a unified viewport. But it is a browser that navigates between content, not a runtime that hosts one experience's running logic inside another with defined containment boundaries and an event propagation protocol.

sources.title: Sneeze Viewport module note
sources.quote: The Open Metaverse Browser is a working browser for spatial content.

coverage.note: The Open Metaverse Browser navigates between spatial content and has some networking for session joining. But it does not define a mechanism for state in one loaded world to cause changes in another world with nobody present. Its role is displaying content, not coupling world state.
